newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone welcomes ousting of rebel leader.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone welcomes ousting of rebel leader.

text.p: Sierra Leone President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah has offered to work with a new leadership of the rebel Revolutionary United Front (RUF) which announced the sacking of leader Foday Sankoh for blocking the peace process.
To judge by the string of callers to state radio and general celebrations in the bars of the capital Freetown, the war-weary general public appear to appreciate the move.
But just who will replace Sankoh, reported to be under house arrest in Nigeria, and the extent to which they will have the backing of rebel commanders in the field remains unclear.
"The reasons given for Foday Sankoh's removal show that the RUF leadership is interested in lasting peace in Sierra Leone ," Tejan Kabbah said in a statement issued by state radio.
"The government is prepared to cooperate with the new leadership for sustainable peace while awaiting further details on the affair," the radio added, quoting the statement.
Captain Philip Palmer, military representative on the RUF's external delegation, announced the ouster of Sankoh on Saturday in the Ivory Coast.
Palmer, a founder member of the RUF, said the decision was unanimous and made after radio contacts with rebel commanders in Sierra Leone.

"For now we are trying to restructure the leadership to fill the vaccum," he told Reuters by telephone from the Ivorian town of Danane, near the border with Guinea and Liberia. "We are in active consultation with our brothers in Sierra Leone."
Palmer, 39, confirmed a report from the Nigerian ambassador in Sierra Leone last week that Sankoh was effectively under house arrest in Nigeria's commercial capital Lagos.
A statement signed by Palmer said that the sacking of Sankoh aimed at "promoting the spirit of healing and reconciliation and a rapid return to normalcy" in Sierra Leone.
"The RUF High Command declares with immediate effect, the leadership role of corporal Foday Sankoh terminated," it added.
Sierra Leone, rich in diamonds and other minerals, is one of the world's poorest nations.

Sankoh, who took up arms in 1991, signed a peace deal with Tejan Kabbah in Ivory Coast on November 30. Implementation has dragged, suggesting that the deal was unravelling. Each side accused the other of truce violations.

Palmer's statement, delivered to Reuter's office in Ivory Coast, denounced what it called Sankoh's "unyielding determination to thwart the peace process and prolong the suffering of the people of Sierra Leone".

The statement said that Sankoh, who had spent most of the past year in Ivory Coast, persistently refused to meet U.N. officials and members of a peace commission who travelled to Abidjan to discuss the implementation process with him.
It also accused him of refusing to nominate members to joint monitoring and demobilising committees.
Officials in Ivory Coast say Sankoh went to Nigeria on a private visit without informing his Ivorian hosts. Nigerian officials say he arrived there on March 2.
Nigeria's ambassador to Freetown, Alhaji Mohamed Abubakar, told Reuters on Wednesday he was under house arrest in Lagos.
Tejan Kabbah took office a year ago after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule.
